questions.q: Match each value to its data type.
questions.feedback: A character is one symbol; a string is any number of them, including one.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 1: Data types

questions.q: Which data type should be used for a variable holding the number of pupils in a class?
questions.feedback: A whole number that will be counted and compared. Storing it as a string would stop it being used in arithmetic.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 1: Data types

questions.q: Explain why a program has to cast the result of an input before using it in a calculation.

markPoints.concept: input is received as a string
markPoints.exemplar: Whatever is typed in is received as a string.

markPoints.concept: so it has to be converted to a number before arithmetic will work
markPoints.exemplar: It has to be converted to an integer before it can be used in a calculation.

questions.example: Anything typed in arrives as a string, even when it looks like a number, so it has to be cast to an integer or a real before it can be used in arithmetic — otherwise adding two inputs would join them end to end instead of adding them.
questions.paraphrase: Keyboard input always comes back as text, which means it must be converted into a numeric type before any sum will work on it.
questions.feedback: What input gives you, and what it has to become.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 1: Data types

questions.q: What does this program print, and why is it not 9?
questions.feedback: Both values are strings, so + joins them rather than adding them. This is exactly what casting is for.
questions.misconception: Expecting 9 assumes they are numbers. The quotation marks say otherwise.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 1: Data types

questions.q: Match each operator to what it gives.
questions.feedback: // is whole-number division and % is the remainder. ** is to the power of.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 4: MOD and DIV

questions.q: What is the result of 17 MOD 5?
questions.feedback: 17 ÷ 5 is 3 remainder 2, and MOD gives the remainder.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 4: MOD and DIV

questions.q: What is the result of 17 DIV 5?
questions.feedback: DIV gives the whole number of times 5 goes into 17, throwing the remainder away.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 4: MOD and DIV

questions.q: What does this program print when 23 items are packed into boxes of six?
questions.code:
total = 23
boxes = total // 6
left = total % 6
print(boxes, left)
questions.feedback: 23 ÷ 6 is 3 remainder 5, so three full boxes with five left over. This pair of operators is how a program packs things into boxes.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 4: MOD and DIV

questions.q: A program must work out how many full minutes are in 200 seconds. Which expression gives the answer?
questions.feedback: DIV gives whole minutes; MOD would give the seconds left over.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 4: MOD and DIV

questions.q: Which comparison operator means 'is not equal to'?
questions.feedback: A single = assigns a value; == compares; != compares for difference.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 5: Comparison and Boolean operators

questions.q: What does this program print for a 15-year-old member?
questions.feedback: The age test fails but member is True, and or needs only one side to be true.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 5: Comparison and Boolean operators

questions.q: What does this program print for a score of 48?
questions.feedback: The first two tests fail and the third succeeds. Once a branch is taken, the rest are skipped.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 5: Comparison and Boolean operators

questions.q: Explain why using = instead of == inside an if statement is a mistake.

markPoints.concept: a single = assigns a value rather than comparing two
markPoints.exemplar: A single = assigns a value rather than comparing two.

markPoints.concept: so the condition does not test what the programmer intended
accept: compare|comparison|compares|comparing|not test|does not test|not what|not comparing
markPoints.exemplar: So the condition does not test what was intended.

questions.example: A single = assigns a value to a variable, while == compares two values, so an if statement written with a single = is not testing anything — in many languages it would also overwrite the variable being tested.
questions.paraphrase: One equals sign stores a value in a variable instead of comparing, which means the condition is not actually checking what the programmer wanted it to check.
questions.feedback: Assignment against comparison, and then the consequence.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 5: Comparison and Boolean operators

questions.q: What does this program print for the word Revise?
questions.feedback: len counts the characters: R, e, v, i, s, e.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 6: String manipulation

questions.q: What does this slice of the word computer print?
questions.feedback: A slice runs from the first index up to but not including the second, so 0 to 3.
questions.misconception: Expecting 'compu' counts index 4 as well. The end of a slice is not included.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 6: String manipulation

questions.q: What does this program print after lowering the case and joining a number?
questions.feedback: lower() makes it lower case and str() turns the number into text so it can be joined.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 6: String manipulation

questions.q: A string holds 'Revise 360'. What does len() return for it?
questions.feedback: Ten characters, because the space counts.
questions.revisitLabel: 2.2 Lesson 2 — Type foundry, station 6: String manipulation
